item.title: Home Depot Has the Best Return Since IPO, and It Isn't From Selling Cheap
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-acquired-home-depot-上市以来回报第一-靠的不是卖便宜货/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-acquired-home-depot-上市以来回报第一-靠的不是卖便宜货/
item.description: It packaged education into retail: a customer asks how to fix something, and the associate stops and teaches. A 25-cent washer leads to a $100,000 kitchen remodel — value that no Six Sigma spreadsheet can manage.
item.content:encoded:
It packaged education into retail: a customer asks how to fix something, and the associate stops and teaches. A 25-cent washer leads to a $100,000 kitchen remodel — value that no Six Sigma spreadsheet can manage.

A three-and-a-half-hour retail case study: the first half is 1970s financial engineering and startup gossip, the second half is a mechanism teardown of decentralization versus centralization and stock-based incentives, at high information density.

1:08 North America only, yet worth more than Netflix
Home Depot has a market cap of $350 billion, the 45th-largest public company in the world, worth more than Netflix, Alibaba, Goldman Sachs and LVMH. David stresses how crazy that is, because unlike those other companies it only does North America. Ben admits he had it wrong at first — he thought home improvement was just a big store in the middle of a shopping center, not a company that matters to the world. The category is far bigger than he thought, and nearly all of its revenue comes from one continent.

2:16 Since its 1981 IPO, it has the best S&P 500 return
Home Depot went public in 1981, a year after Apple. If you had put $1,000 into each and held to today, Home Depot's return would beat Apple's; with dividends reinvested, that is roughly 25% compounded annually over 45 years. It is the single best-performing stock in the S&P 500 from its listing date to today: $1,000 would become about $17 million, versus just $170,000 for the S&P 500 over the same period. David notes that who holds this equity is itself a key part of the company's strategy — early employee ownership and long-term share price growth are the same mechanism.

42:12 Home Depot is not a Price Club clone
What Bernie set out to build was not a low-SKU warehouse club but a warehouse where you buy everything for one job: Price Club carried only 4,000 SKUs, while Home Depot would stock 25,000 and deal with a huge base of suppliers. Gross margin was set below the industry too — hardware retail's standard was 45% at the time, and they ran at 30%. The other fundamental difference is the nature of the goods: anyone buys toilet paper, but nobody is born knowing how to build a deck, install blinds or lay flooring, so the store has to be staffed with people who have real expertise — and Price Club's org structure was never designed for that.

1:26:09 Big-box stores aren't the moat; service is
In the 1980s a pile of capital rushed into the category: Builders Square, Home Club, Home Quarters Warehouse, Mr. HOW Warehouse, all copying Home Depot, and not one of them is around today. David's explanation: Home Depot is not "Costco for hardware." Costco is general-merchandise retail where customers need no human help beyond the checkout lane; Home Depot is specialty retail, where price, selection and convenience — the "trinity" — are not enough, and you also have to offer something unique to the category, just as a tire shop has to mount tires, a beauty store has to let you try makeup, and Apple has to have a Genius Bar. Home Depot essentially invented "serving the customer" in the home improvement category itself.

1:35:12 Low gross margin lives on turnover, not margin rate
Home Depot's warehouse model has two structural disadvantages: an extremely high SKU count and an extremely large in-store service staff, which makes fast turnover operationally hard, and per-store labor cost higher than the price club model. Ben says what holds it all up is "manufacturing buying frenzy" — with that many SKUs you have to give people a reason to buy the whole store. The key line: what feeds the company is not the gross margin percentage but gross profit dollars. So it needs enough volume and enough turnover that the gross profit dollars add up to justify all that inventory in the store. Once volume is there, it can place bigger orders with suppliers, demand lower prices, and pass the savings to customers, spinning the whole wheel faster.

1:53:38 It invented the national chain, so no one could buy nationally
Home Depot's early philosophy was radical decentralization, letting stores use local knowledge to decide what to stock and how much; Bernie estimated this made per-store sales 15% to 20% higher. But at scale the costs of decentralization outweighed the benefits: operational chaos, systems and technology that couldn't be unified, and countless decision-makers and negotiators facing the same suppliers without getting the best price. Ben makes a key point: this problem didn't exist for anyone else, because the very concept of a "national hardware chain" was invented by Home Depot — before it, nobody bought nationally, so there was no national purchasing opportunity to have.

2:12:04 Replacing knowledgeable associates with 16-year-old cashiers
Nardelli replaced a large share of store associates with part-time general-retail labor, effectively killing the whole philosophy of "a knowledgeable person sells you a 25-cent washer, fixes your sink, and brings the big follow-on order." According to Arvind's research, from 2000 to 2006 store staff fell from 200 to 170, a 15% cut. Store-manager standards changed too, with a preference for college-educated candidates — while the associates hired in the stores had no college degrees, effectively telling those people they were locked into jobs with no promotion path. The result: customer satisfaction fell to the lowest among major US retailers, while revenue and profit doubled.

2:20:10 Pay not tied to the stock price means no value stored in the company
Ben nails the incentive misalignment: if pay is tied to the stock price, you don't care about current-period results — you want investors to believe you are storing long-term value in the company, so you keep prices low, push volume, and make customers fanatical; if pay is tied to today's numbers, you don't store value in the company, you just pump today's numbers. David calls it "the paradoxical misalignment of incentives." Nardelli refused to tie any compensation to the stock price, on the grounds that the stock price was the one metric he couldn't control — which is precisely what violated the core of the company model: the associate's promise had always been "I do good work, the stock goes up, I get rich."

item.title: A Bunsen Burner Doesn't Reduce Plate Contamination, and Vegetables Protect the Heart by Another Mechanism
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-thisweekinmicr-本生灯不减少平板污染-蔬菜护心另有机制/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-thisweekinmicr-本生灯不减少平板污染-蔬菜护心另有机制/
item.description: A Bunsen burner may actually increase settle-plate colonies in low-contamination environments; the cardiovascular benefit of vegetables may not run through the nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway but through gut bacteria turning nitrate and iron into DNIC that directly activates sGC.
item.content:encoded:
A Bunsen burner may actually increase settle-plate colonies in low-contamination environments; the cardiovascular benefit of vegetables may not run through the nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway but through gut bacteria turning nitrate and iron into DNIC that directly activates sGC.

The first half has a clean experimental design and a counterintuitive conclusion; the second half's DNIC paper has a complete mechanism but dense terminology, suited to people willing to chew through mechanism.

6:05 A Bunsen burner does not reduce plate contamination
The authors used paired settle plates: one placed next to a lit Bunsen burner, one next to an unlit burner, both exposed simultaneously to the same contamination airflow. The lit burner overall did not lower average contamination, and the statistical comparison showed no significant improvement. This directly challenges the common claim that there is a general sterile halo around the blue flame. The authors do not say the burner never helps; they say the effect depends on environmental conditions — they deliberately contaminated the lab air with Gordonia rubripertincta and then compared different flame sizes and dry versus wet particles.

10:13 83 CFU per minute is the crossover point
Under dry-particle conditions with an average 18 mm flame, they observed an apparent crossover point: when the airborne microbial concentration was above 83 CFU/min, settle plates next to the Bunsen burner tended to show less deposition; below that level, deposition tended to increase instead. This can explain decades of contradictory anecdotal experience: people in dry environments genuinely believe the burner helps, while people in modern air-conditioned labs with low airborne contamination genuinely find the burner useless or even worse. Relative humidity in a typical modern air-conditioned lab is usually between 40% and 60%.

13:43 Airflow is not one-dimensional — don't light a burner in a laminar flow hood
The traditional view is that convection pulls contaminants upward, but the authors point out that the same airflow may first drag contaminated air laterally across the work surface before it rises. Any upward airflow must draw replacement air from somewhere, so the most important thing during aseptic work is to limit wind or airflow. This leads to the most practical point in the episode: there is no reason to light a Bunsen burner inside a laminar flow hood, since the flame itself disrupts the laminar flow. The authors did not directly visualize airflow; they measured a biologically relevant outcome — contamination — rather than fluid dynamics directly, and the authors themselves list this as a limitation.

17:49 Flaming tube mouths and lighting burners are both ritual
The authors draw a historical comparison with the old practice of flaming culture tube mouths. Michael's graduate advisor at the time said stop doing it, there is no evidence it helps, and produced the 1972 paper proving it. The judgment in the episode is: changing behavior is hard, especially when a ritual gives people a sense of control — lighting the burner feels proactive, flaming the tube mouth feels like protecting the culture, but there is no evidence it actually does anything. The authors do not argue for abandoning the Bunsen burner; they argue for measuring: use simple settle plates to measure your own lab's environment and let evidence guide practice.

28:14 Vegetables may protect the heart via the DNIC pathway
This Cell paper proposes reframing the entire nitric oxide synthase pathway: not a local paracrine model (eNOS makes NO that acts on adjacent smooth muscle), but an endocrine-like circuit — nitric oxide synthase makes nitrate, nitrate enters the gut, microbes turn it into dinitrosyl iron compounds (DNIC), which then act on targets such as the heart. If it holds up, the cardiovascular benefit of dietary nitrate (leafy greens, beets) may be mediated mainly by microbe-generated DNIC, rather than the nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway we currently believe in. The author is Andrei Kleshioff at the Karolinska Institute.

31:32 No DNIC can be found in germ-free mice
They used electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) to directly detect DNIC in tissue. Signals were visible in the liver and kidney of healthy mice, but when the same assay was done in germ-free mice, no DNIC at all could be found in the tissue — the first hint that microbes are making it. After feeding inorganic nitrate, liver DNIC levels rose in conventional mice but not in germ-free mice; if ferric citrate was added to the nitrate drinking water, the liver DNIC signal rose even higher, while ferric citrate alone had no effect. The same in vitro: mouse and human feces plus nitrate plus iron can produce DNIC, while germ-free mouse feces cannot.

39:55 DNIC directly activates sGC, not via free NO
They used isolated mouse aortic rings, pre-contracted with phenylephrine, then added DNIC. To distinguish free NO from direct sGC activation, they used two pharmacological tools: one that scavenges free NO and one that directly blocks sGC. The sGC blocker completely abolished DNIC-induced relaxation, while the free-NO scavenger only partially attenuated it. The conclusion is that DNIC activates sGC, but not through free NO — the FeNO2 entity itself appears to directly activate sGC. The same holds for bacteria-generated DNIC: only wild-type E. coli supernatant (anaerobic, with nitrate and iron) relaxed aortic rings, while a mutant lacking nitrate reductase did not.

47:16 DNIC suppresses leucine uptake and holds down mTORC1
On the metabolic side, they measured the phosphorylation state of key proteins in the liver mTORC1 pathway. In disease-model mice, mTORC1 was overactivated, downstream S6K1 phosphorylation was elevated, and transcription factors driving lipid synthesis were also elevated. Both DNIC treatment and nitrate-plus-iron supplementation brought these markers back to control levels. Mechanistically, they used glioblastoma cells to measure radiolabeled leucine uptake and found that DNIC inhibits leucine uptake in a concentration-dependent manner, suggesting it inhibits the leucine transporter — leucine is the key signal telling mTORC1 that nutrients are available, so blocking uptake blocks mTORC1 activation.

item.title: Private Credit's Risk Is Hidden in Insurers' Ratings
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-excessreturns-私募信贷的风险藏在保险公司的评级里/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-excessreturns-私募信贷的风险藏在保险公司的评级里/
item.description: Private credit has poured into insurance companies, much of it in affiliated investments, rated by private agencies that are systematically too generous; on correct ratings, insurers would have to hold an extra $400-500 billion of capital a year.
item.content:encoded:
Private credit has poured into insurance companies, much of it in affiliated investments, rated by private agencies that are systematically too generous; on correct ratings, insurers would have to hold an extra $400-500 billion of capital a year.

The first half is industry lore; the real value is in the middle and back sections — the specific mechanics and numbers on private credit ratings, private equity in 401ks, and Social Security reform.

5:08 A stock fund should be 80-90% stocks
When Bob Posen took over as Fidelity's president in 1995, the firm was in an awkward spot: Jeff Vinick had moved half of the Magellan fund into cash, which both dragged on performance and violated holders' expectations of a stock fund. His approach was to build consensus internally first — if the fund you run is a stock fund, you have to keep 80% to 90% of the position in the kind of stocks the fund's name implies; if you want balanced, if you want money market, the firm has other products. His logic: investors bought this fund's positioning, and a manager cannot change that positioning just because he thinks "now is not a good time to buy stocks." That rule later became basic discipline for Fidelity's stock funds.

8:12 After assets double, keep the startup feel by splitting into small teams
Under Posen, Fidelity's assets under management grew from $500 billion to $1 trillion. His judgment was that the key to managing that much money is not process but how to preserve entrepreneurial spirit and a sense of belonging. The method was to split the investment team into a number of relatively small groups — value, growth, small cap, international — so each group had a stronger sense of ownership over results. At the same time he consolidated money market and bond funds into New Hampshire, because fixed income and money market funds look at the same credits, and here scale is a friend that spreads out enormous economies of scale; stock funds are exactly the opposite.

19:21 Put private equity in 401ks, but cap it at 10-20% first
Posen is reserved about putting private equity into 401ks. The core problem is liquidity: if a participant puts all of their retirement assets into a single private equity fund, they simply cannot get the money out when hit with a medical emergency or when they reach the age for required minimum distributions. His proposal is that private equity can only be part of an asset-allocation fund or a target-date fund, not a standalone option; if it must be a standalone option, employers should set a cap, and the magnitude he gives is 10% to 20%. He draws an analogy to employer stock: GE employees who put their whole 401k into GE stock did not end up well, and a retirement account needs diversification.

21:25 The instant markup in secondary trades is an accounting loophole
Private equity is hard to value to begin with, and what worries Posen most is secondary trades: a private fund, needing to raise cash or nearing the end of its investment period, sells part of its portfolio at a discount to another private fund. There is a technical loophole in the accounting rules that lets the buyer immediately mark that investment up to par on the books, even if it bought at a 5% discount. He thinks this rule has to change. Valuation is already hard enough; this kind of "instant markup" should not be allowed to lift book value out of thin air and pass it through to holders via NAV.

24:28 Private ratings systematically overstate private credit
The private credit held by insurance companies can, on different measures, reach as much as $2 trillion, and a large share of it is "affiliated investment" — starting with Apollo, more and more private equity firms have become owners of insurance companies and then put debt related to themselves into their own insurers. Posen and his co-authors found that a great deal of private credit is rated by private rating agencies, and that rating shopping exists. Two studies, from Columbia and Imperial College, show these private ratings are systematically too high; on correct ratings, insurers would have to hold an extra $400 billion to $500 billion of capital a year. His solution is direct: make the private ratings public and let the market pick apart the assumptions and methodology.

29:35 Mark Walter's $20 billion of affiliated credit is a wake-up call
Posen treats the Mark Walter case as a wake-up call. Walter founded Guggenheim and figured out early that buying a life insurer lets you steer what was a conservative insurance portfolio into higher-yielding securities, including private credit related to Guggenheim or to its own portfolio companies. The rules themselves allow insurers to invest in affiliated private credit, provided it is disclosed to regulators. Regulators have now found that insurers controlled by Walter or Guggenheim hold about $20 billion of affiliated private credit, some of which may have been used to buy the Los Angeles Dodgers and the Lakers. Walter's side is trying to divest part of the affiliated credit. Posen stresses this is not just Guggenheim: large private funds including Apollo and KKR have all found insurers to be a handy investment vehicle.

41:52 Someone with $1 million investable should not hold 40% bonds
Posen points out that most target-date funds are 80% bonds and cash, 20% stocks at retirement, which is reasonable for someone who has to live off the retirement portfolio. But more than 7 million people in the US have investable assets (excluding their primary home) of over $1 million; they do not live off investment income and can ride out a down year in stocks. He calculates that over a 30-year horizon, a 60/40 portfolio and the 90/10 he advocates (90% stocks, 10% cash) differ by a factor of two in terminal value — the equivalent of $5 million versus $2.5 million. He rebuts the objections one by one: over the past 60 years bonds only acted as a hedge in 10 of them; in 2022 stocks and bonds both fell about 18%; stocks fall deeply, but look at two years, five years — after 2008, 2002 and 1974 they recovered and went higher.

50:09 Semiannual reports are fine, but don't scrap first- and third-quarter filings
Posen supports keeping quarterly reporting and opposes moving to semiannual. The reason is that the economy, diplomacy and a company's own circumstances all change fast, and six months is a long time; and the information vacuum created by semiannual reporting encourages insider trading. His compromise: at mid-year and year-end, file full 10-Qs and 10-Ks; in the first and third quarters, file a slimmed-down report, three or four pages plus the income statement and balance sheet — not a big burden. He rebuts the claim that "less reporting encourages long-termism": when the UK made the move from quarterly to semiannual reporting optional in 2013-14, he and a quantitative accounting scholar at Columbia compared the two groups of companies, and the companies that switched to semiannual did not invest more in R&D or capital expenditure.

item.title: Astra crosses the AGI threshold, but nobody can audit it
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-cogrev-astra-跨过-agi-门槛-但没人能审计它/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-cogrev-astra-跨过-agi-门槛-但没人能审计它/
item.description: Astra frees humans from ever doing certain tasks again, yet OpenAI paused only half its RL compute; external audit is structurally locked out until two or three days before release, and there is no adult in the room to take the blame.
item.content:encoded:
Astra frees humans from ever doing certain tasks again, yet OpenAI paused only half its RL compute; external audit is structurally locked out until two or three days before release, and there is no adult in the room to take the blame.

The two hosts chain together the capability evidence for Astra, the true magnitude of OpenAI's pause announcement, why auditing can't get off the ground, and why doomers can't hedge their bets — high information density.

3:30 Astra holds long tasks together with a single notes file
In the past, models handling long tasks compressed a million tokens into a summary and opened a new window, losing all the detail. Astra instead maintains a long-lived notes file that the model updates at any time and carries forward with it, no matter how many tokens have already been written, and it can still search back through its own session history. So the same million-token context window can effectively manage roughly ten times that much context within a single rollout. Nathan calls this a mechanism that is ‘obvious in hindsight, but genuinely new.’

6:19 OpenAI self-reports 3.1 agent workdays per workday
In its research-acceleration blog post, OpenAI gives its own unit of measure, the ‘agent workday,’ and reports that each human workday corresponds to 3.1 agent workdays. Nathan admits the methodology is unclear; his reading is the literal one: for every eight-hour shift a human researcher puts in, the agent runs twenty-four hours in real time. The same post also has a chart grouping by human time spent and looking at Astra's success rate, effectively a substitute for the METR curve. Nathan says the METR curve hasn't been updated in a long time — not for lack of wanting to, but because the tasks aren't big enough anymore: the model iteration cycle is now shorter than the task length that needs to be measured.

21:03 External audit is structurally locked out at two or three days
Prakash breaks down why external audit can't get off the ground: there are a hundred candidates in a model's lifecycle, and the release version is only settled in the final two or three days, so external auditors get only a few days. Bringing the audit team into the company a month early runs into a second layer of problems — audit firms are short on people and money, depend on funding from model companies, and their staff keep flowing to model companies; and if two companies agreed not to poach from audit firms, that would itself be an antitrust problem. He says the revolving-door problem in financial-industry regulation remains unsolved to this day.

31:12 What was announced as a pause actually stopped only half
Nathan reads OpenAI's RL compute chart: what was announced was a ‘frontier scale RL pause,’ but in reality, when the Hugging Face incident was disclosed, half was stopped first and the other half kept running — and that half was already enough for the Astra model to take over part of OpenAI's research infrastructure; even so it wasn't fully stopped, only half was cut. As for whether the remaining blue compute labeled ‘non Astra’ contains a model stronger than Astra, he says he doesn't know, but ‘I've been disappointed before.’ Prakash adds: the real frontier model isn't the one deployed, nor the one being trained, but the one in the researcher's head, because those ideas become models twelve to eighteen months later.

39:05 There is no adult in the room to take the blame
Prakash's rebuttal to Jacob Coxen's line that ‘accepting this race and entering the endgame is an arrogant gamble launched from a private company's Slack’ is: then who do you want to hand it to? Pete Hegseth's Signal group? His judgment is that there is ‘no adult in the room’ — no external savior, the whole world is held together with tape, and most of the smartest, most capable people to handle this are already inside these companies. Hand the decision to the government and what you get is political legitimacy, not wisdom, and not the legitimacy needed to execute. So the starting point has to be accepting that the world is just like this.

46:03 Operation Warp Speed is the precedent for a safe harbor
Nathan proposes the government should set a hard deadline the way you would with a child: you sort it out yourselves, here's the deadline, and if you can't, I come in and play the bad guy. The accompanying move is to first take away the antitrust excuse. Prakash counters with Operation Warp Speed: the pharma companies specifically demanded immunity from vaccine claims, wanted a safe harbor, and actually got legislation; without that exemption, they would have been sued into bankruptcy after the pandemic. So lawyers warning that ‘there will be retroactive reckoning in the future’ is not alarmism — even if all current decision-makers agree, it doesn't matter, because the only thing that binds future decision-makers is law, not the verbal promises of today's people.

1:00:40 FSD's mistake is putting a human in the loop
Raffi has crashed a Tesla using FSD. His judgment is that FSD's interface design is bad, because it claims human in the loop but when it actually hands control to the user it doesn't give nearly enough time to understand the situation and decide what to do; Waymo's design premise is that there is no human to take over, so the safety argument is completely different. He personally would be willing to drive FSD again on the highway, or at least sit behind the wheel, but would be more hesitant on local streets in Palo Alto. The same company also has two kinds of code contracts: the Firefox team only allows humans to commit, while the Mozilla AI team has an entire codebase not a single line of which was written by a human — people only write the spec, and the whole codebase is automatically regenerated when CI builds.

1:29:15 The takeover is already complete, nobody just admits it
The key disagreement between Prakash and Daniel: Daniel hasn't realized this has already happened. The financial market is itself a paper clipper, the means of production is the financial market, and the financial market is already fully fused with AI. Humanity took roughly a hundred years to hand complete control of the means of production to the financial market. He says don't think of AI as a chat box; it's a global information process that doesn't have to run in a single box, and doesn't even have to be silicon-based — humans together with AI agents can constitute this information process. The reason Jacob became disillusioned is that he discovered in the Slack group that there was no control at all, yet he still assumed there existed somewhere in the world a group that could actually make decisions.

item.title: Enterprises will run 80% of tokens through open models, but spend only 20% of budget
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-ycsp-企业最终八成-token-走开源模型-但只花两成预算/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-ycsp-企业最终八成-token-走开源模型-但只花两成预算/
item.description: Open models and closed frontier models are not substitutes: the vast majority of tokens will go through open models, the hardest work stays with the frontier labs, and routing and orchestration connect the two in between.
item.content:encoded:
Open models and closed frontier models are not substitutes: the vast majority of tokens will go through open models, the hardest work stays with the frontier labs, and routing and orchestration connect the two in between.

The Ollama CEO gives first-hand token-flow data: local and cloud model mixes look completely different, and the real constraint on enterprise purchasing is security, not cost.

1:03 The driver behind open models is control, not saving money
Jeff says cost is the biggest pain point open models can solve immediately, but the enterprise north star is "better control over AI and customizing it for yourself." Cost is just the piece that can be solved in the short term; only once it is solved does customizing the model to your own use case come up. The order matters: if you treat open models purely as a cost-cutting tool, you will misjudge why they are spreading so fast inside the Fortune 500. AT&T has already moved 40% of its token consumption onto open models, currently mostly US and European models, while also evaluating Chinese models.

4:05 Two inflection points: coding agents, then OpenClaw
Ollama's per-user token usage curve on the cloud has two clear inflection points. The first came early in the year, driven by coding agents — Kimi, GLM and MiniMax launched in succession, and for the first time open models could carry a coding agent. The second came in April, brought by OpenClaw, as users expanded from developers to non-developers: finance, customer service, marketing and sales can all hand a hard problem to an open model and let it run to completion, picking tools and pulling data along the way, burning enormous numbers of tokens. Context windows growing from 128K to over a million is the technical precondition for this surge.

8:08 Model launch day is a 24-hour fire drill
Ollama is a coordination channel for model vendors ahead of launches, but Jeff says you are lucky if you actually get a model weeks in advance; most of the work gets crammed into the final 24 hours before launch. Three things have to land at once: inference engine support (often weeks of work, to make sure it is fast, accurate and consistent with the reference implementation), the accompanying harness (there are plenty of open-source harnesses now, like Codex and OpenCode), and capacity from hardware and inference providers — launch day is usually the single biggest day of growth. He compares it to an operating system: drivers, the inference layer and the application runtime all have to be glued together, and it is a combinatorial explosion problem.

14:11 Above the token is where the new scarcity lives
Jeff cites three directions from Anthropic's platform team: knowledge (wiring company data and context into the model), coordination (one request spawns a pile of sub-agents, some in the cloud and some local, that need scheduling), and execution (sandboxes and compute). His judgment: tokens are already in oversupply, dozens of open model providers can supply them, and what is scarce is how to orchestrate an agent from A to B on top of the tokens. Following the path of cloud computing, developers ultimately prefer the best standalone product at every layer rather than something packaged together like Heroku or Google App Engine.

17:14 Stateful things will not sink into the model layer
Asked whether the harness will be absorbed by the model, Jeff's judgment is that the core loop and hooks will sink into the model, but a few categories of things cannot. One is the state problem — models are trained on a monthly cadence and can never catch up with the latest data, so storage is a huge standalone problem space. The other is credential management and security. Open models do not come with a whole security toolchain the way closed providers do, and that is critical to enterprise adoption. This explains why the stronger the models get, the more middle layers there are.

18:15 80% of tokens go through open models, but only 20% of budget
Jeff's steady-state judgment: the vast majority of tokens inside an enterprise — his figure is 80% to 90% — will go through open models, but that does not mean 80% to 90% of budget flows to open source. The open community is driving costs extremely low, so maybe only 10% to 20% of spending lands on open models. The hardest work stays with the frontier labs, because that is where the best researchers are; the big middle is open and closed models combined. He uses a law firm analogy: the partner hands work down to a pile of associates.

22:19 Local and cloud model mixes are not the same thing at all
On local models, US and Chinese models are basically neck and neck; on cloud-hosted models, it is almost entirely Chinese models. Jeff says local is a three-way mix of US, European and Chinese models, while cloud coding agents are dominated by Chinese models. The division of use cases is clear too: coding agents write code and tests, hit many hard problems, and mostly rely on large cloud models; end-to-end low-difficulty workflows like document processing run very well locally. So it is a hybrid execution model — simple tasks run locally, plus a router that decides when to go up to a large model.

29:25 The Flash tier is the precondition for unlimited tokens
Jeff says that early in the year open models had just caught up to the intelligence frontier, within less than 3 months of the closed frontier, and the next problem to solve was extreme efficiency. The key metric for models like DeepSeek Flash is not just low cost per token but low cost per task. This tier is good enough for 80% of tasks, fast and extremely cheap, and will become the workhorse doing the grunt work. He recalls that in the ChatGPT era nobody thought about token usage, and we will eventually get back to that state, but it requires model architectures trained specifically for high token volumes. The fastest-growing segment on Ollama's cloud is precisely the DeepSeek line, driven mainly by Flash adoption.

item.title: One Report Closed Over a Hundred Medical Schools, and Black Doctors Were Cut Off for a Generation
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-stuffmissed-一份报告关掉上百所医学院-黑人医生从此断层/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-stuffmissed-一份报告关掉上百所医学院-黑人医生从此断层/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: The Flexner Report is usually written up as the starting point of modern medical education, but it also closed five of seven Black medical schools, and for nearly forty years no new Black medical school appeared.
item.content:encoded:
The Flexner Report is usually written up as the starting point of modern medical education, but it also closed five of seven Black medical schools, and for nearly forty years no new Black medical school appeared.

Medium information density. The first half is a chronological slog through Flexner's life; the real value is in the second half, on how the report reshaped medical education and how it cut off the supply of Black doctors.

6:09 The report's author was not a doctor but an education reformer
Abraham Flexner was not a medical man. In 1890 he ran an experimental school with no fixed curriculum, no exams and no grades, and his students still got into good schools; in 1908 he wrote The American College, A Criticism, attacking American higher education, which is why Henry Smith Pritchett of the Carnegie Foundation came to him and asked him to turn the same critical eye on the medical schools of the United States and Canada. He spent two years travelling to 155 medical schools, recording admissions requirements, faculty, finances, laboratories and hospital affiliations school by school, and in 1910 delivered Medical Education in the United States and Canada. It was precisely because he was an outsider rather than a member of the medical community that the assessment dared to be so unsparing.

14:23 Medical schools were still teaching out-of-date knowledge
In the fifty years before the report, bacteriology, diagnostic technique and surgery were all changing fast, but medical schools had no uniform standards. At many schools the faculty were practising physicians who taught the way they themselves had been taught and did not update the content. The result was that the care the doctors they produced gave their patients was, at best, antiquated and, at worst, life-threatening. Admissions standards were just as chaotic: when the report was published, 74% of medical schools required only a high school diploma, some accepted even a high school equivalency certificate, only one in five required more than two years of college coursework, and many schools were essentially for-profit businesses.

18:31 He recommended closing 120 of the 155 schools
Flexner set standards first and then graded school by school: admission should require college-level biology, chemistry and physics; the curriculum should include classroom and laboratory work in anatomy, pathology, bacteriology and pharmacology; there should be a teaching hospital for hands-on practice; and teachers should be salaried, full-time teaching and research staff rather than physicians practising on the side. He published the results by state and by school, naming dirty laboratories and lax standards, and criticising course schedules that left students sitting for hours, exhausted, listening to dull lectures by part-time instructors. In the end he recommended closing 120 of the 155 schools. Within ten years the number of American medical schools was down to half, the surviving schools reformed their standards and curricula, and laboratory and clinical teaching were modernised on a large scale. In Canada only one school made the closure list, and it ultimately did not close.

23:43 He never did the arithmetic on Black medical schools' books
The report was equally unsparing toward Black medical schools, writing that five of the seven "could make no valuable contribution at this time," and affirming only Howard and Meharry as worth developing. But the assessment did not take into account that Black medical schools charged far lower tuition than white schools, had smaller endowments, and were already running on extremely thin margins. He wrote that "the Negro needs good schools rather than many schools," and said that one of the most important duties of Black people and Black nurses was to teach hygiene rather than life-saving skills — a statement that is itself racist. Every Black medical school he named as inadequate closed: the first four closed before 1914, the fifth in 1915, and the last held on until 1923.

25:48 The next Black medical school would not come until 1966
Howard and Meharry survived and are still there today. But the next medical school primarily serving Black students was Charles R. Drew Medical School in Los Angeles, which did not open until 1966, and then in response to the health-access needs of the Black community; the one after that was Morehouse School of Medicine in Atlanta in 1975. The direct consequence of narrowing the options was a huge care gap: many potential doctors were shut out of educational opportunity by geography, and Black patients were often cared for by white doctors who, even at best, carried inherent racial bias. An expert panel convened by the AMA's Institute for Ethics in 2005 concluded that Flexner's line about "good schools rather than many schools" ensured that medicine remained segregated, and that the communities most in need of doctors were the ones left without them.

26:51 The AMA was paying behind Carnegie's project
One fact not disclosed at the time: the Carnegie Foundation hired Flexner for the project, and the AMA was also a sponsor. There is also an unresolved question — whether someone connected to the AMA accompanied him on some of the school visits. He said different things at different times, sometimes that the person went with him, later that they merely met there, so whether the report was subject to more direct directional influence cannot be determined to this day.

28:53 Did he know he was constraining Black medicine?
He knew. The report contains a passage of idealistic colour, saying that building up Howard and Meharry would benefit the nation far more than barely sustaining more schools. In 1933 he wrote to the board of the institute he had founded, arguing that hiring and admissions "shall not directly or indirectly take race, religion or sex into account." One explanation comes from his biographer Thomas Neville Bonner: when Flexner was growing up in Louisville, the local Black community had more services and opportunities than in many places, with a dozen or so Black schools and vocational training in medicine and law for Black students; the Flexners were not well off, there were Black families among their neighbours, and he and his siblings often played with Black children in the community. This may have left him overly idealistic about the reality of Black family life, and he later admitted that it was not until he began studying educational institutions that he realised how disadvantaged those Black classmates of his had been.

35:01 The hygiene line may not have been his own
The claim that hygiene was the main duty of Black doctors is one of the key pieces of evidence for calling Flexner racist. But the leaders of Meharry and Howard had said similar things in 1907 and 1908 — two or three years before the report — and those leaders were also white. This suggests Flexner's formulation may have been a restatement of the schools' established mission rather than a judgement he arrived at independently. In 2011, Lynn E. Miller and Richard M. Weiss, writing in the Journal of the History of Medicine and Allied Sciences, proposed another possibility: that this language was in fact opening up a public health role for the doctors at these schools, in order to win support across racial divides — because those statements about hygiene being the most urgent need are immediately followed by the conclusion that these institutions obviously ought to be supported. In 2008 the AMA issued a public apology for its history of racial inequality.

item.title: Copper grades have fallen from 2% to 0.4%, while AI's power demand goes to the moon
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-oddlots-铜矿品位从2-跌到0-4-ai的电力需求却要上天/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-oddlots-铜矿品位从2-跌到0-4-ai的电力需求却要上天/
item.description: Global copper grades keep sliding and new mines take 35 years to permit, while an AI search draws 30 times the power of a normal one — supply is shrinking, demand is exploding, and copper is becoming the new oil.
item.content:encoded:
Global copper grades keep sliding and new mines take 35 years to permit, while an AI search draws 30 times the power of a normal one — supply is shrinking, demand is exploding, and copper is becoming the new oil.

Robert Friedland draws on 40 years in mining to lay out copper's supply-demand deadlock: falling grades, 8-year equipment lead times, sulfuric acid shortages. High information density, but the real goods only come in the back half.

14:30 The next 18 years will dig up all the copper of the past 10,000
Friedland offers an arithmetic that makes you squirm: humanity has mined 700 million metric tons of copper in all of history, and to recover all of it you would have to dismantle the US and Europe back to the mammoth age to get roughly 700 million tons back. But at the current pace of the global economy, just sustaining 3% GDP growth — not even counting EVs and data centers — means the next 18 years will require digging up the same amount of copper as the past 10,000 years. And people in the industry broadly think that is impossible, because the US has deindustrialized and hasn't built a single copper smelter or nuclear plant since.

22:51 The world's largest copper mine's grade is falling off a cliff
Friedland dissects Escondida: when this, the world's largest copper mine, was discovered a generation ago, its grade was close to 2%; today it has fallen to 0.8%, and within two years it will drop to 0.4%. Falling grade means crushing and grinding more rock to extract less metal, and crushing and grinding account for 4% to 5% of global energy consumption. The mine sits at 12,000 feet in the Andes, in the Atacama Desert where it hasn't rained in 30,000 years, and it takes two cubic meters of water to crush one cubic meter of rock. They built a $4 billion desalination plant and spend $1 million a day on electricity pumping water from sea level up to 12,000 feet. The upshot: just keeping this one mine producing requires another $10 to $12 billion of investment.

27:54 An AI search draws 30 times the power of a normal one
Friedland gives a concrete energy comparison: one Google search consumes the electricity to light a 100-watt bulb for 12 seconds, while one AI search — he cites ChatGPT4 and Cloud — draws 30 times that, equivalent to lighting a 100-watt bulb for two or three minutes. Every five-year-old on the planet with an iPad is using AI search, and power demand ‘literally goes to infinity’. He also points out: nothing about the internet is inherently green, and this very studio is copper-intensive and energy-intensive.

34:01 Sulfuric acid prices rose more than sixfold in eight months
About 25% of the world's copper needs sulfuric acid for leaching and extraction, and sulfuric acid comes mainly from Middle Eastern natural gas. After the Strait of Hormuz closed, sulfuric acid prices went from $150 a ton to over $1,000 a ton in eight months. Russia and China have already banned sulfuric acid exports. Friedland's company benefits, because it built Africa's largest copper smelter where sulfuric acid is a byproduct — they sell it to fellow copper miners in Congo, at ever higher prices. But he warns: without more sulfuric acid, global food prices will rise too, because sulfuric acid is also used to make fertilizer.

51:25 Buying one large motor means waiting eight years
Friedland tells a supply-chain story absurd in its specificity: building the Oyu Tolgoi copper-gold mine in Mongolia's Gobi, they needed large motors about 40 feet in diameter, and the ring gear alone took four and a half years to arrive. Today the same equipment takes eight to ten years, ‘if ever’. And hyperscalers trying to buy natural gas turbines face lead times of six to eight years. An even more extreme example: a Congo copper mine flooded by an earthquake needed pumps to drain it, pumps moving 1,300 liters per second with a head three times the height of the Eiffel Tower. They called the US and Germany, and neither could build them, because they couldn't get samarium-cobalt magnets. Only China could build them within 30 days. At the time, the flooding was costing $15 million a day in lost revenue.

58:35 US miners earn $100 an hour; Congo engineers earn $800 a month
Friedland directly compares cost structures: Congo copper grades run 3% to 6%, the median age of the population is 18.7, and a Congo software engineer who knows AI earns $800 to $1,000 a month. Mining copper in the US, by contrast, means the United Steelworkers demand over $100 an hour for underground work, plus environmental legislation and legal constraints, making costs far higher. He also criticizes the net present value model invented by the financial system: it was designed for oil and gas, but mines can't be shoehorned into it — an oil field decays fast without investment, whereas a mine with 100 years of reserves won't deplete like an oil field. The NPV model suppresses mining company valuations, and today mining companies' total market cap is under 1% of the S&P 500, the lowest in history.

1:02:39 Tariffs could keep US copper mining alive, but they'd stoke inflation
Asked about copper tariffs, Friedland says explicitly that he won't take a position, but he can argue both sides: if copper is $6 and you add a 30% tariff, that's $1.80, taking copper to $7.80, and then he can afford to pay American miners, making US mining viable. But the other side is domestic inflation, possibly higher interest rates, and with midterms coming, it's a political question. He boils it down to: do you actually want to reindustrialize America? If you can't even build nuclear plants and ships, you lose sovereignty. Last year the US built about 8 ships; China built 1,000.

1:04:42 Governments are quietly stockpiling copper, and no one can tally supply and demand
Friedland raises an overlooked phenomenon: governments are buying copper as a proxy for money, and not reporting it. He says no one can calculate the supply-demand balance for any metal, because ‘why would you’. Meanwhile China is buying gold and selling US Treasuries, and a great debasement trade is beginning. Hedge funds borrow yen and depend on the yen weakening so they never have to pay it back. He thinks we're at an inflection point, where everything is becoming naked and globally scrutinizable.

item.title: Active management giant moves its headquarters to Nashville, saving $85 million a year
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-mastersinbiz-主动管理巨头把总部搬去纳什维尔-一年省下8500万美元/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-mastersinbiz-主动管理巨头把总部搬去纳什维尔-一年省下8500万美元/
item.description: Alliance Bernstein moved from New York to Nashville, saving roughly $85 million a year, and forced no portfolio manager to relocate — the savings are real estate and people costs, the bet is on hiring people New York can't.
item.content:encoded:
Alliance Bernstein moved from New York to Nashville, saving roughly $85 million a year, and forced no portfolio manager to relocate — the savings are real estate and people costs, the bet is on hiring people New York can't.

A 32-year JPMorgan veteran explains the structural shifts in asset management: active to passive, ETFs replacing mutual funds, private credit entering 401ks. Medium information density; the second half is worth more than the first.

9:18 When passive squeezes active, cut costs before talking growth
The Alliance Bernstein Bernstein took over was hitting the biggest industry headwind since the financial crisis: money moving from active to passive, fees compressing across the board, institutional sales commissions falling from 20 to 25 cents a share all the way to a few cents or less than a cent. The firm itself had just been through a collapse — post-merger AUM had touched nearly $900 billion mid-quarter and was down to $380 billion by 2012; in 2006 roughly 70% was equity assets, and by 2012 only 30%. His predecessor, brought in from Goldman Sachs, restructured, replaced parts of the teams, and equity performance began to recover, which is what got the firm back to net inflows. Bernstein says what he brought was not firefighting but a more global perspective and an emphasis on distribution.

21:39 Moving to Nashville saves $85 million a year and forces no one to move
The firm was debating whether it could still afford a New York headquarters, and ultimately chose Nashville from five candidate cities — the reason being that it wanted to be a big fish in a small pond, which it couldn't do in Charlotte or Dallas. The move saves roughly $85 million a year, part real estate and part people costs. The key design: no portfolio manager is forced to relocate, because the firm is a price-taker for that kind of talent. As a result, nearly 100 portfolio managers chose to move. The challenges are concrete too: Nashville is the capital of healthcare services, and it's hard to find international tax accountants and technology and operations people with traditional Wall Street training locally; but the firm received a flood of résumés from Atlanta, Chicago, New York, Boston and the West Coast.

25:44 Sell-side research without cross-subsidy can only be a joint venture
Bernstein says a buy-side firm owning a sell-side research business is a historical accident. Almost every peer uses equity capital markets or prime brokerage to cross-subsidize its research department, and Alliance Bernstein had no such businesses to subsidize with. So they put the research business into a joint venture with Société Générale, and made clear it would eventually transition entirely to SocGen. He specifically mentions the other side's concern was culture — a large French institution facing a group of Americans and Brits — so it had to be done step by step, very carefully. The transition period runs five years from the JV's anniversary, and they are still midway through it.

37:08 Banks are structurally unsuited to holding long-dated fixed-rate assets
Bernstein uses his experience running leveraged finance at JPMorgan to explain the structural opportunity in private credit: banks are highly leveraged players operating on short money, structurally unsuited to holding long-duration assets, especially fixed-rate ones. JPMorgan at the time spent a great deal of time and money trying to securitize its loan book, and credit derivatives started there. Insurance companies and funds are a better home for this kind of asset, because funds don't offer a real liquidity option and therefore have no run risk. He states plainly that there is no maturity transformation in credit, and apart from interest and principal there should never be any liquidity at all.

40:14 Private credit's problem isn't defaults, it's insufficient disclosure
Asked how the industry gets past the first-half troubles this year, Bernstein's answer is education and transparency: tell clients how many names are on the watch list, how many have stopped accruing interest. He says there is currently no mandatory disclosure obligation, but regular updates to clients make them more comfortable, and you should "over-communicate in times like these." He also frames the problem as structural rather than systemic: defaults are simply part of lending, and models typically already build in 2%, 3%, 4% default expectations; what went wrong was a handful of companies, plus fraud, which has always existed; what genuinely went wrong was structure and pricing getting out of balance for a while. His conclusion is that after going through this, now is actually a better entry point.

43:14 Private credit into 401ks: fees are not the obstacle
Bernstein thinks target-date funds and 401ks may be exactly the right place for private credit: demand is highly predictable, professional managers make the decisions, and plan sponsors are themselves sophisticated investors. Alliance Bernstein worked with Brookfield and Carlisle to develop a vehicle that can sit alongside target-date funds, building diversified exposure to private credit, private equity and private real estate. He concedes the industry has been too optimistic about the pace of adoption, that plan sponsors are conservative, and that this will take many years, but in ten years it will most likely be part of large plans. On the fee objection, his response is: these are institutional buyers and they will drive a hard bargain; and private assets are only a small slice of a target-date portfolio, so the impact on total fees is limited.

47:18 Retirement planning should go through retirement, not stop at it
Bernstein points to Australia's superannuation funds as an example, saying they are thought leaders on how to think about retirement, and that one key practice is designing the glide path to go through retirement rather than stop at it. His reasoning: what most people need least at 65 is to hold mostly short-term fixed income and cash, because they may have another 20 to 25 years to live. More practically, many people haven't saved enough to retire, and will delay retirement and look for supplemental income. He also proposes a specific mechanism: rather than buying an annuity in one lump at retirement, design the target-date fund to leave a pool of liquidity at 75 to buy an annuity, which can significantly lower the cost of the annuity while extending income protection over a longer lifespan.

51:26 AB is the last publicly traded partnership
Bernstein says AB is probably the last publicly traded partnership, a structure rare outside energy MLPs. It means issuing K-1 tax forms, and institutions have an allergic reaction to K-1s, which limits their willingness to hold the stock. He describes the stock as "a bond with an equity option," essentially high-yield debt plus an equity kicker. Asked why not change the structure and make the stock pop, his answer is direct: if they changed the structure and the stock didn't pop, a lot of people would be unhappy; and most shareholders would be negatively affected on taxes, so the board has to consider it, but the honest answer is that it's not a sure thing.

item.title: The Oldest Manuscript of The Song of Roland Is Actually an English Performer's Copy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-britishhist-最古老的-罗兰之歌-抄本-其实是个英国人的演出本/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-britishhist-最古老的-罗兰之歌-抄本-其实是个英国人的演出本/
item.description: The Oxford Digby 23 manuscript is written in Anglo-Norman, and scholars date it to between 1140 and 1170 by the degree of dialect drift — the most complete version of this French epic was performed for the English.
item.content:encoded:
The Oxford Digby 23 manuscript is written in Anglo-Norman, and scholars date it to between 1140 and 1170 by the degree of dialect drift — the most complete version of this French epic was performed for the English.

This is a members-only sample episode, medium information density, but it gets very concrete about how a manuscript gets read as "some minstrel's working copy" — good for listeners interested in manuscripts, oral epic and dialect reconstruction.

1:03 The most complete version is an English manuscript
The Song of Roland is a French epic that took shape around the 12th century, belonging to the genre of Chanson de Geste (songs of deeds), and it spread with 12th-century French cultural hegemony to regions including Britain. But its most complete and oldest surviving version is not from France proper — it is an English manuscript, catalogued as Oxford Digby 23. This manuscript was at some point sewn together with a completely unrelated book by a later hand, which is why it is called Digby 23 B, and A is that "other book." Who sewed them together is unknown; possibly some monk felt both were his favourite books.

3:05 Every stanza is a camera position
The poem is organised in laisses (stanzas) of varying length, and each laisse is like a camera focus: when the scene or the mood changes, you change laisse. The whole poem is in decasyllabic meter, cut in performance into four plus six: the first four syllables rise, then a dramatic pause, then the last six syllables fall, overall close to iambic turning into trochaic. Recited over and over this becomes hypnotic, and the poem runs four thousand lines — hours of recitation.

7:27 At peak emotion, the same action is performed three times
This kind of epic has a convention that is very hard for a reteller to handle: when the action is especially intense or the emotion especially strong, it will use several consecutive laisses to tell the same action from three angles, a kind of slow motion in verse. For example, Roland's refusal to blow the oliphant is told three times, with almost no gap between them. This is also why it reads like an action film or a comic: scenes cut hard, with no softening transition — for instance, "Roland dies, his soul ascends to heaven" is followed directly by "the Emperor arrives at Roncevaux."

9:29 The end of the manuscript preserves the performer's name
Digby 23 is very likely a real minstrel's working copy. Line 4002 of the poem, its final line, says roughly: "here ends the song of deeds; Turoldus will tell no more." This line comes before Charlemagne's lament, so it reads more like the performer saying: this is too sad, I cannot go on. The name Turoldus does not appear in the poem, and he is not a known scribe, so scholars lean toward him being the owner of this manuscript, the performer of this performance.

10:31 Pocket-size dimensions give away that it was for work
The manuscript measures only about six and a half inches by four and a half inches, a pocket copy you could carry on your person, not a finely bound volume for a wealthy collector. It is itself heavily worn and not refined, and contains some small annotations of unclear meaning. Together these features point to a professional performer on the move: he might have travelled alone with an instrument, or been the lead singer or narrator of a troupe, with someone in front of him doing the physical performance. Such people were jongleurs — the source of the later word juggler.

12:31 The dialect pins this performer to England
The manuscript is not in the French of central France, nor continental French, but in Anglo-Norman, which suggests this performer was probably Anglo-Norman, performing in Britain or at least in Normandy. The dialect features are very specific: continental French O and OU are replaced by U, so Roland becomes Rulant, l'or becomes l'ur; Anglo-Norman French is also losing final soft e. These changes even begin to break the originally strict decasyllabic meter, leaving some lines with only nine syllables or swelling to eleven.

14:34 Accent drift alone can date a manuscript
Scholars' grasp of this dialect is fine enough that they can date the manuscript to between 1140 and 1170 based on the degree of accent drift. The method is similar to scholars reconstructing Shakespearean pronunciation, tracking regular changes in syllables and sounds. Poetry is especially suited to this kind of reconstruction, because meter and rhyme expose which sounds were dropped and which were added. For many jongleurs, French was a second language anyway, spoken with a dialect accent, and they spelled by sound.

17:40 A French epic, an English artifact
Although this is a French poem about an old French king, the manuscript is an English thing, performed for Britons at the time. There is no other equally complete manuscript to compare line by line, but there are abundant records of The Song of Roland being sung before and after this manuscript, and scholars can use them to judge where this performer departed from what the genre should look like. The episode goes on to cover the poem's symbolic system, how its audience was constructed, and what the music sounded like.

item.content:encoded:
RSI is a cumulative task: in theory a Python file under a million tokens could train a recursively self-improving model from scratch. A law-firm paralegal, by contrast, has to remember shifting interpersonal relationships and tacit ways of doing things — a non-stationary distribution.

The three researchers' disagreements about RSI, continual learning and RL generalisation are very concrete, and the second half's mechanistic explanation of mid-training and signal-to-noise is the most valuable part of the episode.

0:00 A model looks smart, then a month later it looks dumb again
John Schulman describes a recurring loop: a new model comes out, people are blown away and say "this is AGI", but after about a month of use it starts to look dumb again. This loop may keep repeating, and it's hard to predict how many more times. His mechanism: capability doesn't explode right now because you still get bottlenecked doing research and engineering — even if a model can write far more code than a person, that doesn't give you a 100x productivity gain. Dwarkesh opens by asking: if there's no crazy alien superintelligence by 2036, what's the most likely technical reason? Beren Millidge's default answer is a Moravec-paradox-style continuation — AI does superbly at whatever humans put into a benchmark or environment, but a stubborn sim-to-real gap always blocks the rest.

18:39 Distillation is the only force against centralisation
John Schulman sees distillation as the main force countering the centralisation trend: anything learnable through RL can be distilled easily, because the number of bits is small and a little data suffices. But he stresses distillation is not trivial — when you distill with supervised learning the prompt distribution matters enormously, and you need a real, broad prompt distribution. He mentions something that surfaced recently: some Chinese companies may be running router services that let Chinese users access otherwise-blocked US frontier models, and these services collect and sell data, which is an extremely useful dataset for distillation because it gives you a perfect prompt distribution. Charlie O'Neill draws a concrete prediction from this: frontier labs may not have much of an edge left on RL environments.

44:38 RSI is a cumulative task; being a lawyer is not
Charlie O'Neill splits tasks into two kinds: cumulative and non-stationary. RSI is cumulative — in theory a Python file under a million tokens could train a recursively self-improving model from scratch, and once you discover attention, mixture of experts or GRPO you just add it to the training stack without going back to the start. The real world is not cumulative: a law-firm paralegal has to remember the shifting relationships among all the important people in the firm and all the tacit ways of doing things, which is a non-stationary distribution. Dwarkesh's summary: "RSI just happens to be easier than being a paralegal, which is too bad." If labs conclude RSI is cumulative, more compute will tilt that way.

52:00 Continual learning is stuck on catastrophic forgetting
Charlie O'Neill says the outer loop of pouring data into mid-training at large scale and large batch does work, but at the micro level — a model doing several hundred consecutive small updates for one law firm — every method breaks: SFT on successful trajectories catastrophically forgets, and general capability degrades; on-policy distillation pushes that boundary out a bit further but eventually yields too. RL is good at instilling capabilities and bad at instilling knowledge. Beren Millidge thinks this is mainly a technical problem, not a capacity problem: a model of the same size pretrained from scratch on all the data is simply better, and the bottleneck is plasticity and catastrophic forgetting, with no good way to stop old data being forgotten.

59:46 Data explains 12x, architecture only 3.7x
Dwarkesh and Princeton's Jerry Han ran a grid experiment: pairing training recipes and datasets from 2019 to now in every combination, GPT-2 with the latest Ultra-FineWeb, Delphi with an old dataset like Pile, running the whole grid. The conclusion is that data gives roughly a 12.0x compute-efficiency gain, while architecture improvements give only about 3.7x, and at very small scale. Charlie O'Neill says the big internet chunk has already been eaten, useful material won't grow at the same rate, and there's probably only a pile of 0.1% loss reductions left. He notes someone at Epoch estimated 3x per year since 2019, over 2000x cumulative, and the missing 100x probably comes from post-training.

1:03:00 RL needs a curriculum; pretraining does not
Beren Millidge says this comes back to the RL signal problem: RL is currently bad at exploration, and if the model can't get it in 128 rollouts there's basically no progress signal, so RL needs curricula while pretraining needs none at all. Charlie O'Neill adds: the pretraining signal is already in Common Crawl, the problem is just filtering out noise, which can be automated; but once you get to mid-training and post-training the signal simply isn't in the raw data, and no amount of filtering will extract it — there isn't a Millennium Prize proof hidden in Common Crawl waiting to be filtered out. You have to get the bits elsewhere: have people write out reasoning traces, construct environments, or use human data from deployment.

1:18:03 Most of RL's success comes from mid-training
Beren Millidge says what's underrated is mid-training: pretraining on synthetic reasoning data and environments, warm-starting the model to where it has almost completed 80% of the path to the final RL checkpoint, with RL only fine-tuning the policy on top. So it doesn't need to learn these behaviours from scratch, and a few bits per episode suffice. He also stresses that the signal-to-noise ratio of those bits is far higher than ordinary pretraining — in SFT you have to match another model's reasoning process token by token, which pours in too many bits about "how it thinks" and drowns the signal; RL's objective ignores all the other bits and keeps only "did it get the answer right".

1:28:32 One year or three, the difference is long-tail chores
Asked when you could hire a drop-in remote white-collar worker, Charlie O'Neill says if it has to operate a browser, probably a few years; if it can be given Slack and programmatic access, probably a year. Beren Millidge says full generality might be three years, but organisations will actively reshape themselves to be more AI-friendly, so you get 80-90% before then. The substance of the disagreement is the long tail: some chores humans can do will take the model a very long time. Charlie gives the example that the model won't "yell at people" to push work forward — it's too nice. John Schulman points out that human remote workers already vary enormously in quality, and on Upwork it's often hard to get someone doing a software project to take feedback seriously; in some cases the pre-AI version is worse than today's AI.

item.title: The Clippers Used Fake Endorsements to Skirt the Cap, and the NBA's Law Firm Found More
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-moneystuff-快船用假代言绕工资帽-nba-请律所查出了更多/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-moneystuff-快船用假代言绕工资帽-nba-请律所查出了更多/
item.description: Wachtell's independent investigation did not clear the Clippers; it made the scandal bigger: beyond Aspiration, there is a string of fake endorsements funded by the Clippers that ultimately flowed to Kawhi Leonard.
item.content:encoded:
Wachtell's independent investigation did not clear the Clippers; it made the scandal bigger: beyond Aspiration, there is a string of fake endorsements funded by the Clippers that ultimately flowed to Kawhi Leonard.

The first half is dense with sports-scandal detail; the second half — Apollo's "jerk premium" and the Cede & Co stock custody mechanism — is the part that is actually worth money.

2:04 The Clippers used fake endorsements to get around the salary cap
The Clippers first paid millions of dollars to a company called Aspiration Partners, nominally for vague environmental services; Aspiration then paid that money to Kawhi Leonard in the form of endorsement fees, while Leonard did almost no endorsing. When Pablo Torre first reported it, the claim was still disputed, and the Clippers kept denying it, but the investigation the NBA had Wachtell Lipton do basically confirmed it, and found more similar arrangements.

4:09 Even the scoreboard company was pulled in to launder the money
What the Wachtell report found was not just the one Aspiration payment. The Clippers also paid "consulting fees" to companies that provided no consulting services at all, including the company that made the scoreboard for their arena. The method: the Clippers would pay a consulting fee, then call and ask for a higher purchase price on the scoreboard, with the clear expectation that the other side would pass that money on to Kawhi Leonard. The money goes around in a circle, and the ultimate purpose is still to give the star a raise.

7:09 An independent law firm investigation is not there to clear you
Max had assumed an outside law firm's independent investigation was meant to produce a clean bill of health after a scandal, but the Wachtell report made things look worse. Matt offers a more cynical explanation: the classic use of a law firm investigation, under the shadow of a DOJ or regulatory probe, is to hand over some "bad apple" as a scapegoat so the company gets credit for cooperating. But this time there was no DOJ pressure to shut down the NBA, the NBA seems to have given Wachtell a lot of room, and Wachtell clearly had a great time digging.

10:14 Once the DAT premium vanished, the arbitrage flipped direction
Empery Digital was originally an electric motorcycle company, and in July 2025 it transformed into a digital asset treasury company (DAT), stockpiling about $500 million of bitcoin, with its stock at one point trading at a premium to its holdings. The logic: put $1 of bitcoin into a DAT and it becomes $2 of stock. But the premium quickly disappeared and DATs began trading at a discount, so the arbitrage reversed — use $0.90 of stock to buy $1 of bitcoin, buy the DAT, break it up, sell the bitcoin. DAT activism was born.

17:20 Is a shareholder shorting bitcoin disloyal
One of the core disputes in the Empery case: an activist buys discounted DAT stock while shorting an equal amount of bitcoin, making itself delta neutral and earning only the discount convergence. The company argues this must be disclosed, because the other shareholders are all theoretically long bitcoin, while these people are bitcoin neutral, their interests are not aligned, and they should not be eligible to run for the board. Matt thinks this argument is "wrong, but only accidentally wrong": if the DAT is a vehicle for believers to hold bitcoin (like Strategy), it makes sense; but most DAT shareholders are the same hedge funds, all of whom came for the premium and are unhappy about the discount, so their interests are actually aligned.

23:26 Cede & Co holds most American stocks
Matt mentions in his column a fact most people do not know: most shares of most American companies are registered in the name of Cede & Co, which is DTC's nominee. A 1998 report said Cede & Co held 83% of all US stocks; DTC now custodies about $74 trillion of stock. When you hold shares through Robinhood, what actually happens is that Robinhood has a record on DTC's ledger, and Cede & Co is on the company's shareholder register. This system grew out of the efficiency revolution of the 1960s and 70s, when paper stock certificates were centralised in one place and only name changes were recorded.

27:31 Robinhood's tokenisation is not an on-chain shareholder register
Tokenised stock can mean many things, and one ideal version is this: every company maintains a public blockchain shareholder register, no longer needing intermediaries like DTC or Robinhood, and the company can build a direct relationship with its shareholders. But that is not what Robinhood did — it bought AMC stock itself, then issued derivative securities on-chain representing that stock and sold them to overseas investors, effectively "making its own share of AMC." AMC's Adam Aaron was unhappy, and Vlad Tenev shot back, "What's the concern?"

31:35 Apollo pays 100 basis points for its "aggressive" reputation
A paper measures private equity sponsors' reputations in three ways: having ChatGPT and Claude rank the most aggressive PE firms; looking at who has done liability management exercises (quasi-forced debt swaps); and putting Apollo alone in one bucket and the other 24 firms in another. The conclusion: the most aggressive sponsors' portfolio companies borrow at noticeably higher yields, Apollo's loans are about 100 basis points more expensive than other sponsors', and the average yield in the sample is 717 basis points. Matt calls it the "jerk premium" or the "aggression premium" — creditors expect to be squeezed, so they charge upfront.

item.title: The foldable isn't the future of the phone — it's a two-in-one for a subset of people
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-cn1b5ef7-折叠屏不是手机的未来-是给一部分人的二合一/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-cn1b5ef7-折叠屏不是手机的未来-是给一部分人的二合一/
item.description: Foldables have sold into the tens of millions, but the inner screen gets opened less than 30% of the time. They won't replace the slab phone; for people who want a phone-plus-iPad two-in-one they're a plus, and for everyone else they're a minus that costs you grip and performance.
item.content:encoded:
Foldables have sold into the tens of millions, but the inner screen gets opened less than 30% of the time. They won't replace the slab phone; for people who want a phone-plus-iPad two-in-one they're a plus, and for everyone else they're a minus that costs you grip and performance.

A solo episode with a product manager's eye that covers the real experience of using a foldable, the business logic behind Apple entering, and the judgment that phone form factors will diverge rather than converge. Medium information density; the back half is worth more than the front half.

12:17 The foldable's home turf is China and nowhere else
In 2025, China's full-year foldable shipments broke ten million units, with Huawei taking 70% — a crushing share. But globally, China is the single largest market, accounting for more than 40% of shipments. In other words, this category isn't evenly distributed the way other phone form factors are; its core users are the Chinese bosses holding Huawei foldables in first class and at social occasions. From the big picture, foldables are only 2.5% of global phone shipments, and only 15% of Huawei's own phone shipments.

20:23 The inner screen gets opened less than 30% of the time
Liu Fei used foldables as his daily driver for the better part of a month, and in the end he didn't want to keep them. The biggest problem wasn't the crease, wasn't the camera, wasn't the battery — it was the scenario. The inner screen doesn't get opened much: it's unstable in one hand and prone to shaking, and it's more for situations where you're holding it with both hands — but in those situations he'd already be bringing a 10-inch iPad. A Vivo vice president said at a launch event that foldables keep getting better, but the core way you use them is no different from seven years ago, and many users use the inner screen less than 30% of the time. His analogy: it's like carrying a phone case with a built-in power bank — your phone's weight goes up permanently, but most of the time you don't need to charge, so you'd be better off carrying a separate external power bank.

23:25 Once it gets wider, scrolling feeds actually gets worse
To accommodate the outer screen, wide-expanding foldables like the Huawei Pure X Max and the Apple iPhone Door got wider, and the experience of scrolling feeds becomes very bad. Xiaohongshu is fine, because it's been adapted; but when you're scrolling Meituan to filter restaurants or Taobao to filter shops, the amount of information each screen can hold suddenly shrinks. This isn't purely an adaptation problem, it's an aspect-ratio problem: list feeds run vertically, so widening is meaningless — the height shrinks, and you can see less at once. He recalls that ordering takeout on Meituan, he could only see three restaurants at a time.
